author: krzysztof-smartdataengines
body:
Closes roadmap **#82**, which the new `integration-tests` job found on its **first run**. The window it described turned out to be the smaller half.

## The larger half

`handle_primary_lease_lost()` told the Engine to demote **only** when it could read a leader key carrying a non-empty address:

```cpp
auto state = coordinator_->get_cluster_state();
if (state.has_value() && !state->leader_address.empty()) {
    handler_.demote_to_replica(state->leader_address);   // ← the only call
}
```

After a revoke there is no key, so there is no address, so **the Engine was never told**. `FailoverManager::role_` went to `REPLICA` while `Engine::node_role_` stayed `PRIMARY`, `read_only_flag_` stayed unset, `ROLE` kept answering `PRIMARY <epoch>` — and the node went on accepting writes until it happened to stand for election again, **indefinitely if it never did**. Not a 3.3-second window: an open-ended one.

That is pitfall 28 — *"when a role moves, every component that answers questions about it has to be told"* — in the very path pitfall 28 was written about. Not knowing where to point the replication client is a reason to start no client; it is not a reason to keep claiming a role.

## What enabled everything else

`get_cluster_state()` returned `std::nullopt` for **four** unrelated reasons: not connected, an empty HTTP response, a key that genuinely was not there, and a body that would not parse. A primary reading that as "the key is gone" would step down on every transient etcd error — so it read it as "no information", and therefore could not react to the key actually disappearing. The same conflation made an unreachable coordinator look exactly like a vacant key on the replica side, so replicas campaigned because a *read failed*.

`read_leader()` answers `Present` / `Absent` / `Unavailable`. Everything below depends on that distinction existing.

## The changes

| | |
|---|---|
| Coordinator | says what it does not know (above) |
| Holder | steps down on a **confirmed** absent key — within its 1 s poll instead of `lease_ttl/3` |
| Holder | steps down after a whole TTL with no confirmation, whatever the reason: the lease has had time to expire. Never fires on a healthy node, which confirms every second |
| Holder | demotion reaches the Engine **unconditionally** |
| Candidate | waits out the holder's step-down bound before claiming a vacated key (`--election-lease-wait-ms`, deriving from the lease TTL) |
| Replica | no longer campaigns on a read that failed |

A **cold start does not wait** — no leader has existed to wait for, read from the epoch, which is persisted. The residual hole is a brand-new node that has never seen this cluster's epoch and reconnects during the vacancy: narrower than what this closes, and named in the roadmap rather than left to be found.

## Cost, which was the decision rather than a side effect

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| Failover after `kill -9` | 10.2 s | **20.1 s** |
| Two nodes accepting writes after a revoke | open-ended | **0** |
| Old holder still answering `PRIMARY` | until it re-promoted, or for ever | ~1 s |

Failover roughly doubles, **every time** and not only in the unlucky case. The alternative that costs no latency makes a primary read-only during a brief etcd hiccup, so the cost was moved onto latency deliberately.

## Tests

**744 C++** and **136 integration** tests green. Nine new C++ tests: five on what a read of the leader key means — each of the five cases separately, because the whole point is that they stop being one — and four on the wait as a function of time, pure like `decide_election()`.

`test_a_primary_that_lost_its_lease_refuses_writes` is the one that matters, and it asserts a refused **write** rather than a reported role: a role is what a node says, a refused write is what protects the data. Verified by mutation — restoring the `if (!new_primary.empty())` makes it fail.

**Three existing tests had to be rewritten first**, because they asserted transient states this change re-timed:

- `..._stops_holding_the_role` waited for "exactly one primary", which is true *before* the transition as well as after — so its loop declared success while nothing had happened. It watches for the holder's claim to change now.
- `..._after_a_lease_scare` broke on the first sighting of one primary and then re-read state to assert on it; a prompt step-down widens the race between those two reads. It confirms twice, a second apart.
- `test_no_two_nodes_hold_the_role_at_the_same_instant` was `xfail(strict=False)` from the day CI reproduced the window. It is an ordinary test now, and the suite has **no xfail left**.

The integration suite runs 7:39 rather than 5:41, all of it the deliberate wait across several failover tests.

author: dfadeeff
body:
The live tutor answers every message with *"Das klingt spannend! Aber gerade üben wir. Sollen wir weitermachen?"*. That is not the tutor — it is the `NoModelAvailable` fallback wearing the off-topic line, which means **no model call is succeeding in production**.

Two fixes.

**The error message was actively harmful.** It blamed the child's question for a server problem, and it hid the failure from anyone trying to debug it. It now says plainly that Mika cannot answer, that it is not the child's fault, and to tell an adult. The `done` event carries `error: "no_model"` and the failure is logged with a stack trace.

**`/api/config?probe=1`** makes one minimal real call per configured provider and reports the actual error text. The plain `/api/config` only proves a key is *present* — a revoked key looks perfectly healthy there right up until something calls it, which is exactly the failure this is for.

Also neutralises the palette: `#fbfbfa` is a warm off-white that reads yellow on a display with Night Shift or True Tone enabled.

99 tests pass.

author: jss79
body:
Closes #239 — the sixth bullet of #62, parked since v0.4.0 because there was no sidecar to report a cost. #428 closed yesterday, so the input exists.

## Measured first

Against LiteLLM `main-stable`, with the conformance rig's fake upstream:

| | `x-litellm-response-cost` | `-input` / `-output` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a model it can price | `0.00011385` | `3.3e-05` / `3e-05` |
| a model it **cannot** price | **absent** | `0.0` / `0.0` |

Two things fall out and both are load-bearing. The **bare header's presence is the "priced" signal** — summing the siblings would turn "nobody priced this" into "priced at nothing", and every deployment running a model its gateway has never heard of would show a permanent disagreement with its own table. And the figure goes small: a nine-token embedding costs `1.8e-07` USD, which is **180 nano-USD and a zero at the price table's micro-USD** — a zero that already means something else. So the reported cost is carried in nano-USD, and the difference in units is stated where it is defined.

`packages/litellm-conformance` now asserts all three against a live sidecar rather than a fixture.

## The path

`completion/reported-cost.ts` reads the header (one rule for both adapters, beside `served-model.ts`) → `CompletedTurn.costNanoUsd` → an optional field on `SpendReport` → `drift-db.ts`, beside the counts it priced.

- **One row per `(day, channel, model)`.** Cost is linear in the counts at a fixed price, so pricing a day's summed counts *is* the sum of pricing each turn — it even removes a truncation. The file stays bounded by days rather than growing with traffic.
- **The computed side is never stored.** `node dist/drift.js show` derives it when asked, from the table as it stands then — `PriceTable`'s own rule that cost is computed fresh rather than accumulated. Correct a price, run it again, and the difference is gone over spend already recorded.
- **Only what somebody priced is in it.** No cost → not a disagreement, not recorded. A reported *zero* is recorded, because that is a statement. No model → nothing to compare against.

## It never enforces — three structural things, not a promise

1. The route holds a `DriftRecorder` whose one method writes. There is no read to make a decision from.
2. An ESLint rule forbids `enforce.ts` from importing the store at all (verified firing).
3. The command has **no exit code** for a difference of any size, so nothing downstream can come to depend on one.

`e2e/src/cost-drift.test.ts` makes the claim in both directions, because a negative claim is the easy one to fake — a build ignoring the figure entirely would pass a one-sided case:

- a gateway reporting **100×** the cost refuses nothing (3 calls, 3 `ran` rows, `+9900%` in the record);
- a gateway reporting **almost nothing** does not save a channel from its own table's cap (2 `ran`, 1 `refused`, on the price table alone).

Both read the record back through the real `dist/drift.js`, which is also #239's third acceptance bullet.

## Operator surface

```
docker compose run --rm proxy node dist/drift.js show            # every model
docker compose run --rm proxy node dist/drift.js days claude-sonnet-4-6
```

```
claude-sonnet-4-6           1284 turns  computed $4.1230  reported $4.6010  +11.6%
  your table prices this model below the gateway. A channel's daily_usd is allowing
  more real spend than it reads.
```

The direction is the actionable half, and it is asserted as prose in the tests, not just the arithmetic.

`PROXY_DRIFT_DB` is its own file beside the meter — `budget reset` discards counters and staleness is a property of a table over weeks. Optional on the attempt store's argument, shipped set in compose, so on is the deployment default and off is an edit.

## Two things worth a reviewer's eye

- **`SpendRecord` gained a `day`**, so the observation lands in the day the meter filed the counts under rather than in one a second clock chose. Only shows in the last millisecond of a day, which is exactly when it would show.
- **Upgrade order is still proxy-first**, now for a second reason; `deploy/README.md`'s section is rewritten to say so rather than leaving #62's wording to cover a field it predates.

## Checks

- `pnpm lint`, `pnpm boundary-check`, `pnpm license-check` — pass
- Full suite green per package: schema 654, agent 354, gateway 243, memory 456, cli 140, proxy 1275, proxy-server 237, runner 110, test-kit 49, atomic-write 21
- `e2e` 154 passed, 1 skipped (the documented `github-live` skip)
- `litellm-conformance` 7 passed against a real sidecar, including the two new header cases
- `site/` builds, `astro check` 0 errors

author: edloidas
body:
Search knew where the next hit was but never how many there were, so the badge could only say `Match at line 4211` — no total, no ordinal, no sign that matches existed outside the viewport. `LogLineIndex` now holds a match index beside the filtered view, built one bounded slice per request, and the badge reads `3 of 147 (+58 hidden by filter)`.

- New `action=matches` returns `{total, levels, scanned, lines, complete}`; the client re-calls while `complete` is false, so the request loop is the scheduler and no background thread is needed
- `action=search` returns the count around the hit, with `ordinal` its position among the matches the active filter admits
- Once a scan covers the file, Next and Previous are a binary search over line numbers rather than a file scan, so the monitor hold from #90 largely stops occurring
- A slice matches outside the index monitor, copying blocks out under it as `search` has since #90; its deadline is checked after a block, never before one, since a deadline shorter than one block would return having scanned nothing and the client's loop would never end
- A scan stops short of a line the file has not terminated — the filtered view has to show that line, but a match verdict on a half-written one is what the next byte can overturn

The scan is keyed per query rather than as the MRU-of-one `maskCached` uses. That policy is safe for the filtered view because `filteredIndex` rebuilds inside a single monitor hold, but a match scan is built incrementally across many requests, so two readers counting different queries on one file would evict each other every slice and neither would finish.

- A scan still in progress is never evicted; a newcomer past the cap is refused with `503 SEARCH_BUSY`, bounding the cost to whoever arrived last rather than restarting everyone from line 0
- `foldMatches` verifies the query key, not just the cursor — otherwise a slice matched outside the monitor lands in another query's scan, and `searchIndexed` then serves navigation from it without ever running the matcher
- Counting has its own thread pool with its own stranded-thread accounting, so speculative work cannot refuse an interactive search, and a full pool says so instead of claiming the pattern timed out

The level mask is deliberately not part of that key. Matches are physical line numbers and `levels[]` already holds each line's level, so the response carries the per-level split of every match and the client sums it against whichever filter is active — toggling a level costs no rescan, which matters because toggling is exactly when a reader is counting. The ordinal is mask-scoped, so a hit does not outlive the filter it was found under.

- The client verdict trio `noMatch` / `matchLine` / `hiddenLine` collapses into one discriminated union
- The count starts when a reader runs a search, not on every keystroke: a count reads the whole file, and one per keystroke turns a 13-character query into 13 whole-file scans
- Mirrored in `dev/mock-api.ts`; covered in `LogManagerTest`, the controller tests and the route tests

The match line array stays on the server — a query hitting most of a 300k-line file would be megabytes of JSON to deliver a number. Client-side highlighting is unchanged and remains scoped to rendered rows.

Closes #98

author: jimisola
body:
The skill was written from one org's onboarding. Doing a second one — and then migrating it — surfaced three things it got wrong or left out. Each cost a red sync to find.

## The big one: the admin repo must be public

The skill recommended a private `.github-private` as the admin repo. That arrangement has a hole: **repository rulesets are a paid feature on private repos**, so a ruleset targeting the admin repo answers `403 Upgrade to GitHub Pro or make this repository public`. The repo that declares the organization's protection was the one repo those rules could not protect — and because safe-settings fails the *entire* run on one plugin error, asking for it turns every sync red.

`ADMIN_REPO=.github` instead. Publishing the config gives nothing away: rulesets, labels and repository settings are already world-readable through the API on a public repo, so the file that produces them reveals nothing the API did not. Actions minutes are unmetered there too.

This changes the script default (`--admin-repo`), the `gh variable set` / `gh secret set` examples, and the reference layout.

## One plugin error fails the whole run

Not just the offending repo. A red run does **not** mean nothing applied — on the run that found the 403, the labels, the auto-merge setting and the required checks had all already been written. Worth knowing before you go looking for what got reverted.

## `LOG_LEVEL: debug` is not optional

At the default level, a run that reverted a setting and one that did nothing produce identical two-line logs. With NOP mode crashing in 2.1.18 there is no preview either, so debug logging is the only account of a run you get. It named the 403's repo and plugin on the first try.

## New section: rulesets and bots

A `bypass_actors` entry exempts that actor from **every** rule — required status checks included — not just the review requirement. A bot with `bypass_mode: pull_request` plus `automerge: true` therefore lands dependency bumps that were never green, silently, because the PRs look normal and merged. Three failing builds reached a sibling org's `main` that way before anyone noticed.

The section covers the fix: renovate-approve for the review, `platformAutomerge: false` so the merge waits on the whole branch rather than the required subset, and the fact that renovate-approve does not retroactively approve PRs open at install time.

## Also

Suborg guidance now says to split by **what CI a repo actually has**, since a required check a repo never produces blocks every PR on it forever — which is what forces a product/meta split rather than one ruleset for the org.

## Verification

- `claude plugin validate .` → passed; script re-parsed after the default change.
- Every claim here was observed on a live org today, not reasoned from the docs: the 403, the partial-apply-on-red-run, the silent default logging, and the bot bypass merging red PRs.
- Note: the `-p` smoke test from `/tmp` is unreliable for this plugin — an unrelated `github-tools` plugin in another installed marketplace shadows it by name, and the session resolves that one instead. Validated by structure and by reading the files rather than by asking a session to describe them.

body:
## La causa profonda del recupero password che non arriva

Continua dalla PR #134 (che correggeva un testo fuorviante nella stessa schermata). Il codice arriva davvero su Telegram, ma non al contatto giusto — ed ecco perché.

I **Chat ID Admin** (e in generale qualsiasi impostazione generica: nome del GAS, config EmailJS, link app...) si salvano tramite `syncToSupabase()`, un percorso **diverso** da quello già corretto in passato per prodotti e raccolte (che invece mostrano un avviso bloccante quando la sessione è scaduta).

Se la sessione admin è scaduta — scenario già noto: con email+password la password non resta in memoria, e il token del proxy dura 24 ore — `syncToSupabase()` non ha un token per scrivere tramite il proxy autenticato, e cade su un ripiego: una scrittura diretta con la chiave anonima, **bloccata per certo** dalla sicurezza del database (RLS, da quando la tabella `config` non accetta più scritture anonime). L'unico segnale di questo fallimento era un toast che sparisce in 3 secondi.

**Risultato pratico**: si modifica un Chat ID Admin in Impostazioni, sembra salvato (resta visibile nel browser, scritto in locale), ma il valore non arriva mai al server. Quando il recupero password legge i Chat ID dal server per mandare il codice via Telegram, trova ancora quello vecchio — il messaggio parte comunque (Telegram conferma l'invio, per questo l'errore introdotto nella correzione precedente non scattava: dal punto di vista del server è tutto regolare), ma verso un contatto che non è più quello giusto.

## Correzione

Quando manca del tutto un token di sessione, si salta subito il ripiego (è bloccato per certo, tentarlo è solo rumore) e si mostra lo stesso avviso bloccante già usato per prodotti e raccolte: *"🔒 Sessione scaduta — la modifica NON è stata salvata... Esci e rientra, poi ripeti la modifica."*

## Verifica

Due scenari testati in un browser reale: sessione scaduta (avviso bloccante mostrato, nessuna scrittura tentata inutilmente) e sessione valida (salvataggio regolare tramite il proxy, nessun avviso). 2/2 superati in entrambi.

author: gosha70
body:
T4.4: the presentation seam, on the render surface T4.3 built. Two commits — the packaging fail-fast you signed off, then the seam itself.

All four consequences you pinned are implemented, and the mutation you asked for is a test in both lanes.

## Prepared state, not a retained callback

Every callback is evaluated at the call that installs it or supplies data — `setPresentation`, `renderTrack`, `renderEvents` — against what is already desired. **All preparation completes before any renderer state is mutated.**

That clause is the whole design, and it is stronger than transactional stored state: a marker rebuilt before a later callback threw has already lost the focus a keyboard user was holding, and no rollback brings it back. So a throwing callback rejects the operation with *nothing reconciled* — no marker created, removed, or rebuilt.

Your mutation is a test at both levels:

```
presentation A, event mark E present
setPresentation(B)
  B returns a different anchor for E   ← would force a rebuild
  B then throws preparing a later mark
⇒ A remains desired; E's element is the same element; zero constructions, zero removals
```

The browser version stamps `data-original` on the surviving element first, so a rebuild is detectable rather than merely a re-render.

## Reuse: identity *and* anchor

| Change | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Same key, same anchor | Reuse element, reapply name/class/content/colour/size, move |
| Same key, different anchor | Remove marker, construct a new one |
| Class, colour, size, name, markup | Refresh — never rebuild |

This is the branch T4.3 removed as unreachable. Every built-in mark's anchor follows from its kind, so a key that reused an element always described the same kind of mark; a consumer-supplied presentation is exactly what ends that guarantee.

## `setPresentation(null)` and suppression

`null` restores the neutral built-ins **immediately**, not at the next render. A callback returning `null` suppresses that mark — a decision, not an absence, so the engine's own does not appear in its place.

## Line styling

Data-driven, folded into each feature and read by a `coalesce` expression: one layer per segment would mean a hundred layers for a track with a hundred pauses. `dashed` is the one property MapLibre will not data-drive, so it gets a second layer filtered on the same feature property.

The same prepare-then-mutate rule applies — a callback failure never leaves half the segments styled under the prospective presentation.

## Snapshots

`renderTrack`/`renderEvents` keep deep clones, which `setPresentation` re-derives from. T4.3 removed the retained inputs to stop an unrelated call rereading a caller's object; a presentation change legitimately needs to re-derive, so the retention is a clone rather than a view. Callback *results* are snapshotted too, per your rule 2.

## Mutations

Eight, and the two lanes catch different halves:

| Mutation | Unit | Browser |
|---|---|---|
| Retain the callback, evaluate during reconciliation | **fails (2)** | — |
| Apply each event mark as it is prepared | **fails** | — |
| Commit the presentation before preparing | passes | **fails** |
| Reuse regardless of anchor | **fails** | — |
| Ignore a `null` return | **fails** | **fails** |
| `setPresentation(null)` waits for the next render | **fails (4)** | — |
| Retain the caller's style instead of snapshotting | **fails** | — |
| Retain the caller's track instead of cloning | **fails** | — |

The third row is why both lanes exist: with no track rendered there is nothing for a split commit to churn, so the unit case cannot see it, and the browser case can.

## Two of my own tests were too weak on the first pass

Recorded because the pattern is worth remembering, not for absolution:

- Mutating a returned style after render is **invisible until something reapplies it** — the first render already wrote the then-current values into the DOM. The case now triggers an unrelated reconcile, which is exactly when an aliased style would surface in production.
- The browser rejection case threw from callbacks that never ran, because it rendered a track with no laps and no events. It now renders an event, so the throwing callback is one that actually executes.

Both were found by mutation, not by reading.

## Verification

- `npm run verify` — 843 tests across 38 files
- `npm run test:browser` — 24 tests
- `npm run check:packaging` — clean, and now exits on lockfile drift in 0s instead of reaching the registry

author: xmap
body:
## Summary

Step 2 of the status-page work (Steps 1 and 3 landed as #741 and #742): today REWIND can only show a run if arcturus happened to push it into the relay's 20-run ring since the relay's own last restart — under 1% of the real 2-BM record. This adds an on-demand path over the same outbound socket the live feed already holds open, so a browser can scrub any run, not just a recently-active one.

- **Producer side** (`cora.api._status_push`): a single reader task per connection parses inbound `run_history_request` frames onto a bounded inbox; the existing tick loop stays the sole writer, draining a capped number of requests after each snapshot send (`status_push_request_max_per_tick`, default 2, `0` disables the reader entirely). The one rule that matters most: an `UnauthorizedError` (or any exception) from a request-triggered read is caught and turned into an `"unauthorized"`/`"error"` response — it must never escape into the tick loop's own reconnect handling, or a browser could force the beamline's whole live feed to drop and reconnect just by requesting a run it can't read.
- **Relay side** (`infra/status-relay/relay.py`): a pending-request registry (capped, with a producer-restart epoch check), and HTTP Basic auth on every path but `/ingest` (`STATUS_RELAY_VIEWER_USER`/`PASSWORD`), added because `/run-history/<id>` now reaches the whole record rather than a bounded cache. First automated test coverage `relay.py` has ever had (`infra/status-relay/test_relay.py`, stdlib + websockets only, matching the relay's own dependency posture).
- `docs/stack/deployment.md` and the two systemd unit files updated for the new env vars and the changed verify command (now `401` unauthenticated, `200` with `-u user:password`).

**Deliberately deferred, not silently skipped:** a dedicated seeded identity for the `SYSTEM_PRINCIPAL_ID` reads this module makes (flagged in the module's own docstring as a pre-existing debt); this on-demand path widens that debt's practical exposure without changing its shape. Called out in the docs' Deferred table rather than bundled into this already-large PR.

Not deployed to arcturus/lyra yet — this lands on `main` only; deployment is a separate, explicit step.

## Test plan

- [x] `apps/api/tests/unit/api/test_status_push.py`: 61 tests green, including the two load-bearing cases — snapshot cadence resumes after a slow on-demand read completes, and an unauthorized on-demand request never disconnects the producer (asserted via connection count staying at 1).
- [x] `infra/status-relay/test_relay.py` (new, 9 tests): viewer Basic-auth gate, producer bearer-token gate unaffected, on-demand round trip + cache-after-disconnect, unauthorized→502, not_found→404, producer-restart fails pending requests immediately, too-many-in-flight→503 with `Retry-After`.
- [x] Live smoke test against the real `relay.py` process (not just the test harness) confirming the full round trip.
- [x] Full unit + architecture fitness tiers green (34,332 architecture tests, 1,742 unit tests in `tests/unit/api` + `tests/unit/infrastructure`), unaffected outside the touched files.
- [x] ruff, ruff format, pyright, tach all clean.

## Summary

Two repository configuration changes.

`ExportPackageReleaseNotes` ran only when the caller supplied `ReleaseNotesExportPath`, so every local preview had to invent an absolute path. The property now defaults to `release-notes.txt` in the project's intermediate output: the target runs with no arguments, creates the directory if the project was never built, and prints the file it wrote. The release workflow keeps overriding the property.

`RCS1261` (resource can be disposed asynchronously) joins the Roslynator block at `warning`. Like every rule listed there it is disabled by default, so the severity line is what turns it on: a synchronous `using` over a type that also implements `IAsyncDisposable` now gets reported, which is the same stance as the `CA2007` rule already taken for library code. Nothing in the tree trips it today.

Enabling the rule changed the shared ruleset, so the `VERSION` marker in the header moves to `2.2` and drops the note about superseding `.globalconfig` VERSION 1.3. The other four pet-toys packages stay at 2.1 until the rule is synced across them, which is what the marker is there to show.

body:
Vervolg op #177. Na die merge was Campina goed en toonde Alpro geen € 6.181,74 meer, maar het was nog steeds Barista en nog steeds een pot.

## Waarom #177 niet genoeg was

Ik heb nagemeten wat de nieuwe zoekterm per regel werkelijk oplevert:

| ingrediënt | oude zoekterm | nieuwe zoekterm |
|---|---|---|
| `Alpro` | `alpro` | `alpro mild creamy` |
| `Picnic Appelmoes` | `appelmoes` | `appelmoes` |
| `Snack Tomaatjes` | `snack tomaatjes` | `snacktomaatjes` |

Bij appelmoes verandert er dus **niets**. Ons eigen product heet "Picnic appelmoes", en omdat de winkelnaam als ruiswoord wegvalt blijft er precies hetzelfde woord over als de ingrediëntnaam. Het rangschiksignaal op naam hielp daar evenmin: élk product met "appelmoes" erin scoort even hoog.

## Wat er nu bij komt

**1. De verpakkingsvorm telt mee in de volgorde.** Losse porties horen bij losse porties, een pot bij een pot. Zodra de naam niets meer onderscheidt is dit het enige overgebleven verschil. Gemeten met de echte functie:

```
zonder signaal:                      met ons product (8 x 100 gram cupjes):
  AH Appelmoes      | 720 g            AH Appelmoes cups | 4 x 100 g
  Hak Appelmoes     | 350 g            AH Appelmoes      | 720 g
  AH Appelmoes cups | 4 x 100 g        Hak Appelmoes     | 350 g
```

Onbekend telt nooit als verschil — dan weten we het simpelweg niet, en dat is geen bewijs van het tegendeel.

**2. Twintig zoekresultaten in plaats van tien.** Bij een breed begrip als "appelmoes" staan de cupjes makkelijk op plek twaalf, en wat we niet zien kunnen we ook niet kiezen.

## Wat dit niet oplost

"Snack Tomaatjes" blijft "niet gevonden" bij Albert Heijn: daar heet het **snoeptomaat**, en die twee woorden delen niets. Dat blijft staan tot er een richting gekozen wordt die betekenis begrijpt in plaats van letters.

Let ook op: de nieuwe zoektermen werken pas ná een verversing. De rangschikking werkt meteen op wat er al opgeslagen ligt, maar een product dat nooit is opgehaald kan ook niet bovenaan komen.

## Getest

- 2 nieuwe tests: de appelmoes-volgorde met én zonder het vormsignaal, en dat een onbekende vorm nooit als verschil telt.
- `npm run verify` groen: 631/631.
- `npm run test:e2e` 42/42.

Geen migratie nodig.

author: alexensimag
body:
## Summary

This replaces the standalone context/intelligence-infrastructure research note from #41 with a consolidation into EOKS's existing research and architecture documents.

### Why this replaces #41

#41 captured useful academic/community evidence, but introduced a parallel taxonomy around “intelligence infrastructure”. This PR integrates the useful material into the existing EOKS concepts instead of creating another architectural layer.

### Consolidation

- **`research/context-evaluation.md`** is now the canonical experimental methodology for context, context acquisition, execution state and evidence-provider interventions.
  - Adds the model × repository × task × intervention × budget matrix.
  - Separates productive agent exploration from avoidable information acquisition.
  - Adds execution-state experiments independently from context compression/memory.
  - Adds model-substitution and repository-maturity experiments.
  - Adds an explicit community → academic → replication → EOKS evidence hierarchy.
  - Preserves contradictory evidence rather than assuming retrieval, graphs, context management or agentic search are superior.
- **`research/context-quality-model.md`** now distinguishes context quality, context acquisition and execution state, and adds model/repository dependence and progressive-disclosure hypotheses.
- **`docs/context.md`** clarifies the conceptual boundaries between context, acquisition and execution state and makes the empirical/non-prescriptive stance explicit.
- **`docs/research-agenda.md`** consolidates the new research directions into the existing agenda rather than creating a new workstream/file.

### Concepts deliberately not promoted to architecture

The PR does **not** conclude that:

- graphs are better than raw exploration;
- retrieval is better than agentic search;
- more context is better;
- context compression is always beneficial;
- execution state should replace exploration;
- sub-agents are better than a capable single agent;
- infrastructure makes cheaper models equivalent to frontier models;
- planning is a universal bottleneck.

These remain hypotheses to test.

### Central principle

> **Treat every infrastructure capability as an intervention whose value depends on the model, workload, repository, budget and baseline.**

The objective is to discover which capabilities improve trustworthy software-agent outcomes, under which conditions, and whether their benefit justifies their complexity and cost.

This PR intentionally contains no new standalone `intelligence-infrastructure` document. “Intelligence infrastructure” remains useful vocabulary for grouping research topics, but not an EOKS architectural layer.

Adds a bounded, read-only physical-hardware preflight for the X1 NUC test without overlapping installer implementation, first-boot, Arena, or AI model-selection lanes.

- verifies UEFI boot mode and 64-bit firmware when exposed
- verifies x86_64 and minimum memory
- reports root source/filesystem so the operator can distinguish live-media vs installed phases
- enumerates candidate disks without selecting, mounting, partitioning, formatting, or writing them
- checks EFI variable access, DRM graphics presence, and a non-loopback network interface
- emits an explicit `destructive_actions=0` summary
- adds a static safety contract that rejects destructive disk/mount/power primitives
- adds a dedicated CI gate

This script does not claim hardware validation. It is a preflight designed to catch wrong boot mode, missing hardware, or phase confusion before the destructive X1 install run.

author: potatogim
body:
Part of #2330.

Ports the hipObject v2 reliable-connection session core into `cuwrapper/rc` as the foundation for an RC data plane on vgwrdma. The port covers the session table and state machine, the hipobj-rc-v2 wire codec and request parsing, QP/CQ lifecycle with INIT/RTR/RTS transitions, staging MR registration, the data phase (RDMA write with immediate for GET, receive with immediate for PUT), injectable clock/randomness sources, the RDMA token codec, and a dlopen-based ibverbs shim.

The sources stay close to the upstream hipObject v2 core so the trees can be diffed during review. A Makefile rule builds the objects into `rdma/librcserver.a`; the archive is not linked into any binary yet, that happens with the ABI and binding PRs up the stack.

Merged tree: **34 files, 0 deletions**, 2 modifications (both the ORION-05 runner and its digest file). All five touched `SHA256SUMS` verify clean from the repo root.

## The ORION-05 change is the substantive one, and it corroborates this session independently

It hardens the runner's **authority semantics**:

> Any `start>0` or limit-truncated invocation is a shard and **MUST** emit `PARTIAL_SCAN__NO_STAGE1_AUTHORITY`. A shard may discover candidates, but it cannot certify the globally first three without an external aggregation of the complete earlier prefix.

That is precisely the constraint this session's sharded census run hit, arrived at from the other direction. It is why that run's terminal is `PARTIAL_SCAN_INCOMPLETE` — **18 of 33,755 rows** with both C1 and C2 — rather than a result.

It also adds a preflight workflow and pins `EXPECTED_DOMAIN=33755`, `EXPECTED_RAW=38760`, `EXPECTED_DISTINCT=5005`, and adds an early-stop rule so a `start=0` scan halts as soon as three positive-gap controls are found.

**Verified after merge:** the ORION-05 smoke still performs **0 solves** and confirms the 33,755 repeated-target domain — the Mac-legal invariant holds.

## Note on ORION-05's real cost

Measured on billy-old from 46 timed C2 solves: mean **2,333 s** against **5.83 s** for C1, extrapolating to **~21,878 core-hours** for the full domain. The COMPUTE_PLAN's upper estimate of ~16,900 core-hours was right. This is genuinely allocation-blocked work, not something a laptop finishes.

author: singhharsh1708
body:
`AdaptiveRadau(threading = true)` with a matrix-free Jacobian is nondeterministic once the method has two complex stage pairs: ten solves of a 200-point heat equation at `min_order = max_order = 9` with `KrylovJL_GMRES()` gave ten different answers, spread 1.4e-3 apart at tolerance 1e-7, with one Julia thread they agree exactly.
Every `ComplexWOperator` is built from the same `W1.jacvec`, so the stage solves that `@threaded` runs in parallel all push through one `JVPCache` and race on its pushforward buffers and its product tally; the threaded `nf` came out 566 where the serial solve counts 163.
When threading is on and the Jacobian is a `JVPCache`, `build_complex_W` now gives each complex stage its own operator, `firk_new_J!` moves those operators with the real one, and the existing per-stage drain picks up their tallies, so ten threaded solves now agree to the bit and report the serial `nf`.
The new test checks the operators are distinct, that repeated threaded solves agree, and that the threaded and serial `nf` match; the FIRK Krylov file passes on four threads.
AI Disclosure: Claude assisted with this change.

author: cawlumm
body:
Adds a Claude review workflow that runs on every PR.

## Why

Six slices have come off #150 so far and **exactly one got an independent review**. That
one found a font regression I'd shipped: taking `index.css` from a stale branch reverted
#152's three `@fontsource` imports, so every custom face in the app fell back to system
fonts — with tsc, lint, three unit suites and the whole of CI green. The other five merged
unreviewed, which on a one-maintainer repo means unreviewed by anyone.

## Why this and not the managed product

[Code Review](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-review) — what `oven-sh/bun` uses, where
`claude[bot]` reviews every PR with no workflow file — is **Team/Enterprise only** and bills
**$15–25 per review** as usage credits on top of the plan.

This runs the same `code-review` skill via GitHub Actions, authenticated with
`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, so cost comes out of the subscription's included usage.

## Hardening

Follows what Bun does on its Claude workflows rather than the minimal docs example:

- **Actions pinned by commit SHA**, not tag — a tag can be repointed, and these steps see a token
- **`persist-credentials: false`** so checkout doesn't leave the token in `.git/config`
- **`permissions: contents: read`** at top level, raised per job only where needed
- **`timeout-minutes: 20`** and a **concurrency group keyed on the PR**, so a rapid re-push
  replaces the running review instead of queueing behind it
- **Skips drafts** before starting a runner

Two lines are load-bearing and easy to lose:
- `--comment` — without it findings go only to the workflow run log
- `--allowedTools` — the action starts the inline-comment MCP server only when `claude_args`
  names the tool, *even though* the skill's own frontmatter already declares it

## Before it works

Two things I can't do — both involve credentials or repo admin:

1. Install the [Claude GitHub App](https://github.com/apps/claude) on this repo
2. Add the secret, without the value touching a shell history or a transcript:
   ```bash
   claude setup-token          # prints a token
   gh secret set CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN   # prompts for it
   ```

Until both exist the workflow fails on auth and does nothing else. Advisory either way —
nothing here gates a merge.

## Testing it

`pull_request` workflows run from the PR's merge commit, so **this PR reviews itself** once
the secret exists.

author: slmingol
body:
## Summary

Allows operators to assign a human-readable label to an unmanaged switch port declaration, so the topology node shows a meaningful name instead of the auto-generated `unmanaged@dev:iface` string.

**New syntax** (backward-compatible):
```
PATCHBAY_UNMANAGED="core1:1/0/12,k8s-switch=sw1:1/0/8"
```

The legacy `dev:iface` form is unchanged and still produces `unmanaged@dev:iface`.

## Changes

- **`config.py`** — parser handles both `label=dev:iface` and `dev:iface`; type widens to `list[tuple[str | None, str, str]]` (label is None when absent)
- **`normalize.py`** — `_place_endpoints_and_infer` / `normalize` accept the 3-tuple; named devices use the label directly; prune step handles direction-sorted links (both a_/b_ orientations) and evicts stale nodes in both directions: declared→undeclared and inference→declared
- **`web.py`** — topology label falls back to "unmanaged" for auto-named nodes, shows the custom label for named ones
- **`.env.example`** — documents the new syntax

## Tests

**`tests/test_config.py`** — 3 new tests:
- [x] Legacy `dev:iface` format produces `(None, dev, iface)` tuples
- [x] `label=dev:iface` format carries the label through
- [x] Mixed valid + malformed entry warns and skips the malformed one only

**`tests/test_normalize.py`** — 4 new tests:
- [x] Labeled declaration creates the device under the custom name, not `unmanaged@`
- [x] Legacy `(None, dev, iface)` still creates `unmanaged@dev:iface` device
- [x] Removing a port from the declaration prunes its device and link
- [x] Pre-existing inference node is evicted when the operator declares the same port

All 131 non-snapshot tests pass.

Second-pass static-analysis experiment for the exact FRITZ!Box 7590 / FRITZ!OS 8.25 firmware image.

This pass emits sanitized structural metadata only: ELF architecture/build IDs/interpreters and dependency edges; binary-to-topic associations without raw strings; init/service image-path dependency edges; configuration-persistence reference locations; Web endpoint identifiers plus nearby HTTP-method identifiers; page identifiers; Lua/JS module dependency edges; and filesystem/topology statistics and hashes.

The workflow asserts the exact known firmware SHA-256 before analysis and deletes all AVM payloads/extracted files before uploading the report.

author: ykus4
body:
A correctness sweep across the pass layer, the runtime, the test suite and the
docs. Sixteen commits, each one thing, each with the evidence in its message.

The short version: **three passes did not work, one platform had no test
coverage, and eleven of twelve integration tests were comparing two binaries
neither of which had been obfuscated.** Those facts turned out to be connected.

## The passes that did not work

**`-kagura-pac` produced a binary that crashed on its first indirect call**, on
every target without hardware PAC — x86-64, armv7, plain aarch64. `tagGlobal`
emitted the slot holding an *untagged* `ptrtoint(fn)`, because a ConstantExpr
initializer cannot reference a key that does not exist until run time. The
constructor drew a random key, published it, and never touched the slots. Call
sites, 250 lines away, unconditionally compute `slot ^ kagura_pac_key`. So the
call jumped to `real_pointer ^ random64`. Measured: exit 138 (SIGBUS) before,
runs correctly after. The hardware path had the corresponding runtime store all
along, which is how the two halves drifted unnoticed.

**`opt -passes=kagura-pac` was a no-op** — and so were `kagura-sv`,
`kagura-honey`, `kagura-ci` and `kagura-wstr`. Each re-checked its own enable
flag inside `run()`. Those flags default false and are only set by the clang
driver, so requesting the pass by name — the entry point every lit test and
every `opt` invocation uses — made it decline. `Utils.h` documents this exact
bug and says not to do it; the fix had been applied to eleven function passes
and stopped there. This is why the PAC bug survived: `link_kagura-pac` asks
`opt` for the pass, gets an unmodified module back, links it, and passes.

**`kagura-cse-break` did not implement its transform.** The header describes
XOR-masking so "GVN / EarlyCSE cannot re-merge them"; `cloneAt` re-emitted the
operation verbatim and the RNG parameter was spelled `/*RNG*/`. `opt
-passes=early-cse` collapses the clones in one step. Now implemented, one exact
modular identity per opcode, differential-tested over 225 input pairs × 3 seeds.
The header states what it measurably does and does not resist — a full `-O2`
still folds it, which is fine given the pass runs on OptimizerLast and is a real
limitation under LTO.

## Silent miscompiles

**`kagura-fla` erased a `switch` in the entry block along with all its edges.**
The screening loop rejected `indirectbr` and `invoke` and stopped there. Any
other terminator fell through to an initial state of 0 — no block's case value,
so the dispatcher takes its `unreachable` default. A `switch` in the entry block
is ordinary at `-O2`, and the result was a function undefined for every input.
Case values were also drawn with no collision check and handed to `addCase`.

**`kagura-bcf` built its opaque predicate over a compile-time constant.** It
splits the block, which moves every real instruction into `bcf.orig`, and then
looks for an integer value in what is left — PHIs it skipped by hand, allocas,
and a branch. So it returned its `0xCAFEBABE` fallback essentially always and
emitted `(0xCAFEBABE | ~0xCAFEBABE)`.

**Unmasked random draws abort the compiler.** `APInt Key(PtrBits, RNG.next())`
on a 32-bit target. Reproduced against an armv7 triple with a plugin built
without `NDEBUG`: `Assertion failed: isUIntN(BitWidth, val)`, exit 134. It
survived because the assertions CI job runs on macOS/arm64 only.

**Six "don't touch my own output" guards were dead in every shipping
toolchain.** They tested `BB.getName().starts_with("kagura.")`, and clang
enables `-fdiscard-value-names` by default whenever LLVM is built without
assertions. Measured through `opt -discard-value-names`: block names surviving
0, metadata markers 6.

Also: five passes lied to the analysis manager about what they preserved or
mutated; `SymbolMapPass` ran *before* `VTableProtectionPass` under a comment
reading "run last so all obfuscated names are already in place", so the symbol
map never contained the VTP renames; `kagura-opt -O0` called a pipeline builder
that asserts `Level != O0`, taking out `-kagura-o0-protect` from the tool the
docs name as the supported Windows entry point.

## The runtime

`-kagura-anti-tamper` **could not link on Linux, Android or Windows**:
`kagura_self_check` and `kagura_runtime_hash_check` are emitted on every
non-Wasm target and were defined only in an `if(APPLE)` file. That same
Apple-only file contained an entire Android root-detection block behind `#if
defined(__ANDROID__)` — four functions declared in `internal.h` that `nm` on the
pre-change archive confirms were **never once compiled**.

Plus: a call to a misspelled function that breaks the Android build;
`kagura_symbol_interposed()` returning 1 unconditionally on macOS, so the check
terminated every clean process; shift-by-64 UB in two table protectors,
triggered by any count that is a multiple of 64; a replay-protection bypass for
nonces over 64 characters; both signal handlers calling `sa_sigaction` after
testing `sa_handler` (the same union member); a crash handler advertising signal
safety while calling `getenv`, `snprintf`, `ctime` and `dladdr`; an
environment-controlled unvalidated file write from that handler, which fires on
`SIGABRT` — what `kagura_on_tamper_detected()` raises; `/proc/self/maps` lines
dropped at 4 KB chunk boundaries; `DT_STRTAB`/`DT_SYMTAB` dereferenced without
the ELF load bias; a 65 KB stack buffer; and `getrandom()` with no API guard,
which breaks any Android build below API 28.

## Why none of this was caught

**The whole suite runs on macOS.** All five entries of the LLVM 17–22 matrix are
`macos-14`. The one Linux job that runs `ctest` configures with
`KAGURA_FORCE_STATIC_PLUGIN=ON`, and `tests/CMakeLists.txt` had an early
`return()` for that case — so Linux registered **4 tests, not 73**.

**Eleven of twelve integration tests obfuscated nothing.** Making `REQUIRE_IR`
mandatory exposed it: the subjects were `static` helpers called with literal
arguments, so `-O2` inlined and constant-folded them into a `printf` of four
literals before `opt` ran. "Obfuscated output matches baseline" held by doing
nothing at all.

**Checks that could not fail.** `EXPECTED` was documented, passed from ten call
sites, and never read. The regression corpus ran without `,verify`. The CI
assertion guard grepped a file without checking it exists, so a generator rename
would make it report success — the exact failure the job exists to prevent. Two
lit tests were satisfied by their own untransformed input.

**`find_package(Kagura)` could not work.** The install rules named an export set
that was never installed; no config or version file existed anywhere in the
tree, so the release tarballs shipped no CMake package at all.

Fixed: a `linux-loadable` job running the whole suite; the early return replaced
by a driver abstraction (a static-plugin build now registers **71** tests, with
the two genuine skips printed); a vacuity guard that runs `opt -passes=verify |
FileCheck` over every lit file and fails if it succeeds; `KAGURA_REQUIRE_LIT`
replacing two grep-based guards; a real `install(EXPORT)`, verified by building
an out-of-tree consumer against the installed prefix.

## Docs

Every hand-written JSON policy example named keys the loader cannot read — it
maps `-` to `_`, and unknown keys were discarded with no diagnostic. The worst
case is `docs/cookbook/sdk-vendor.md`, which tells the reader an SDK must not
crash on detection and then writes `"anti-debug": false`; the key was ignored,
so `"profile": "STRONG"` shipped exactly the binary the page warned against. The
loader accepts both spellings now and diagnoses unknown keys by name, with
`-kagura-config-strict` to make it fatal.

`include/kagura/runtime.h` did not exist though five pages tell readers to
include it — added, and installed. Seven more cited functions do not exist or
have the wrong signature. `-kagura-bbcheck` was in the README threat table and
rated "Medium" in `security-m

author: metafrogmeme-droid
body:
Draft. First tranche of a repository-wide audit; the wider pass is still running and more will land on this branch.

Four defects, each with a regression test that fails against the code as it was. `audit/` carries the finding register, the environment-variable diff and the component inventories — including the candidates that were **refuted**, and why.

## What is fixed here

### 1. The GDPR account purge never deleted the bot's user record — HIGH

`bot/web/user_gateway.py` reached for the store as `getattr(tg_handler, "user_store", None)`. `TelegramHandler` has no such attribute; it binds the store as `self.users` (`bot/skills/telegram_handler.py:846`), which is what every other call site in that same file already uses — `_is_admin_id` (`:94`), `_web_skill_denied` (`:148,156,162`), `_guard_user` (`:193`).

So the probe resolved to `None` on every real request. `user_record` became `"error"`, `ok` went `False`, and the endpoint answered **409 `{"purged": false}`** — for every user, on every request. Reproduced by driving the real handler:

```
stores = {..., 'user_record': 'error'}   result = PARTIAL
```

with the record still present in the store afterwards.

On a right-to-erasure path the operator was told the request *partly* failed, with nothing separating "a store refused" from "that line never ran at all".

**Why the existing tests passed the whole time.** `tests/test_account_purge.py` proves `UserStore.forget` deletes from memory and disk, and `test_every_per_user_store_is_named_by_the_purge` scans the handler's source to confirm every store is *named*. Naming a store is not reaching it. The new test drives the real handler and asserts the record is **gone from the store afterwards**; its fixture deliberately does **not** define `user_store`, because a fake carrying both names passes whichever one the code reaches for — which is how this stayed invisible. A second test keeps the genuine `error` branch reachable so the check cannot go vacuous.

This changes behaviour on a compliance path, from "never deletes" to "deletes". It restores the endpoint's documented intent rather than setting new policy, but it is called out explicitly for review. **The fix is not retroactive** — records that survived earlier erasure requests are still there and may need a one-off sweep.

### 2. `guard_lint` accused third-party code in any virtualenv not named `.venv` — MEDIUM

`_COVERAGE_SKIP` matched two hardcoded names while `_route_module_coverage()` `rglob`bed the whole tree. A venv built as `.venv-audit/` produced nine accusations against `matplotlib`, `pandas` and `mplfinance`, because `ax.add_patch(` matches the aiohttp signature `\.add_(get|post|put|delete|patch)\(` as readily as `router.add_get("/path", …)` does.

Reproduced both directions: venv in tree → exit 1 with 9 false accusations; the same venv moved outside the repo → exit 0, all 12 rules pass.

A virtualenv is now whatever holds a `pyvenv.cfg`, pruned during the walk, plus `site-packages`/`dist-packages` for `pip install --target` trees. `.gitignore` had the identical two-name gap. The rule also got ~8× faster by no longer reading the venv.

This is the failure the script exists to prevent, pointed the other way: it warns that a guard nothing reaches is not a guard, and a guard that fires on library code is worse, because the cheapest way to make it stop is to stop believing it.

### 3. `guard_lint` scanned Python comments and docstrings as code — MEDIUM

`_strip_js_comments` exists because a commented-out `router.use(authMiddleware)` once satisfied a rule. The Python branch had no equivalent — and it caught this very change: the comment written to explain fix 2 had to name `ax.add_patch(`, and `guard_lint.py` promptly reported **itself** as an unchecked HTTP surface registering two routes.

This is independent of virtualenvs. Any first-party file whose prose mentions `.add_get(` would be accused, in CI.

Added a `tokenize`-based `_strip_py_comments` that blanks COMMENT tokens and docstrings while **preserving offsets** — the fastapi pattern is `^`-anchored under `re.M`, so a decorator must keep its line and column. Argument strings are untouched, so real route paths still match.

### 4. `tests/test_no_read_only_fields.py` had the same vendored-tree blind spot — LOW

`_py_files` skipped only `__pycache__` and `/.git/`, so an in-tree venv put 107 `site-packages` symbols into the comparison and failed the test on `_pytest.ReprTracebackNative.extraline` — a field in pytest itself. Same structural test. Runtime 130s → 7.9s.

A sweep of all nine tree-walking test/script files found only this one and `guard_lint` walk from the repo root; the rest scope to `bot/` and are unaffected.

## Validation

| check | result |
|---|---|
| new + changed test files | 13 passed, 7 passed |
| `-k "gateway or purge or erasure or user_store"` | **169 passed** |
| `guard_lint` on the real tree, venv present | exit 0, all 12 rules |
| `guard_lint` with a planted rogue route module | exit 1 — still catches it (mutation-checked both ways) |
| `scripts/ruff_gate.py` | 1258 findings, == baseline |
| `scripts/mypy_gate.py` | 648 errors / 77 files, == baseline |
| `ruff --select E9,F821,F811` / `F401,F541` | pass |

Full-suite and `preflight.py` runs come with the next tranche, on a quiescent tree.

## Not fixed here — raised for a decision

The audit's most serious finding is **not** in this diff, because fixing it needs a coordinated two-sided deploy and that is the maintainers' call:

**`POST /api/auth/validate-token` is unauthenticated and takes `chat_id` from the request body** (`app/auth.js:867-889`), writing it straight onto the row's `telegram_id`. `app/auth.js` declares no `router.use(...)`, and `server.js:318` mounts it bare. Any registered user can mint a link token for their own row (`/link-token`), then bind **someone else's** Telegram id to their own account.

`app/lib/identity.js:18-27` then resolves the bot identity from that column — under a docstring that states "the browser can never choose who it acts as". It is resolved server-side, from a row the browser chose the contents of. `app/routes/credentials.js:79-81` gates the exchange-credential path on exactly the two fields the attack sets, then writes `pending_credentials` keyed on the victim's telegram id.

The repo already has the right mechanism and uses it everywhere else — `BOT_SYNC_SECRET` via `X-Bot-Secret` (`app/routes/sync.js:69`, and the "X-Bot-Secret authed" endpoints at `:534,578,699,786`). `/validate-token` is the one bot-channel endpoint that does not use it, and the bot currently sends no such header (`bot/skills/user_middleware.py:200-208`). So the fix is: **bot side first**, then enforce server-side — deploying the server half alone rejects every real `/link`. Details and a proposed patch are in `audit/verified_findings.md` (RC-2026-001).

Also raised, not fixed: 90 boolean flags that **default to ON** — i.e. each is a protection that `false` removes — appear nowhere in `.env.example`, among them `UNPROTECTED_GUARD_ENABLED`, `SLIPPAGE_GUARD_ENABLED`, `PER_STRATEGY_NOTIONAL_CAP_ENABLED` and `LLM_DIRECTION_GUARD_ENABLED`. The defaults are correct; the gap is that they can be disabled through variables the configuration documentation never names. Inventory in `audit/safety_flags.md`.

author: com-junkawasaki
body:
http-service: serve a kotoba/app vertical slice, not a seventh predicate

The first application-shaped slice on `:js-kotoba-v1`: a guest that holds
product semantics as `state + event -> next-state`, with the host holding
mechanism only. ADR-2608261100 demotes decision-core extraction to a
fallback licensed only when a NAMED backend cannot admit the value, and
names this backend as one where the fallback is not licensed:

    wasm / web / `:js-kotoba-v1` に対して、最初から判断核へ潰さない。
    そこでは application を application として書く。

So nothing here returns `:bool` to a host that then decides what it meant.

## The application

`examples/approval-queue-app.kotoba` is a governed approval queue exporting
`init` / `step` / `view` -- the same contract `runtime/dom-driver.mjs`
drives for `examples/todo-app.kotoba`, with the screen replaced by a socket.
It reads its own request body, which is what `kotoba-lang/json`'s
`json_scalar.kotoba` (ADR-2608292330) unblocked; the scanning algorithm is
carried in the module because this host seals and loads one module per
route.

It is an amu-side REFERENCE application, not a port: `server.clj` has no
approval-queue endpoint, so it replaces nothing. What is real in it is read
byte-for-byte out of `cloud-itonami/cloud-itonami-app`, which this commit
does not modify and only ever read:

  * veto beats a satisfied minimum (`approval_core.kotoba`'s `status`);
  * a decision bound to different content does not count (same file);
  * dedupe-by-actor and an `:ignored` bucket for refusals
    (`work_governance.cljc`'s `approval-state`).

That third one is the point. `approval_core.kotoba`'s own header says the
folding stays in `work_governance.cljc` because "those are collections" --
true when the core sat beside a JVM that owned the socket. `:js-kotoba-v1`
admits collections, so the fold moves into the guest.

## The host

`runtime/http-service.mjs` gains `apps` beside `routes`. The host carries
the state between requests and never reads a field of it: it bounds the
value (string, byte ceiling, syntactically JSON) and hands it back
unexamined. Read-modify-write is synchronous with no `await` between
reading the cell and assigning it, so concurrent requests cannot interleave
inside it. State is a `:string` because fuel is a per-instance budget, so a
`:document` cannot cross from one instance to the next.

## Fuel

Measured, not guessed. `scripts/approval-queue-fuel.cljs` bisects the
artifact's `fuel=N` literal against the worst case the host admits -- an
eligible decision whose fields sit behind a structurally-skipped nested
member, at a 1024-byte body and a 1024-byte state. Worst-case minimum is
55820 units; the guest ships at 262144, 4.70x that. The script FAILS if the
artifact is below the measured minimum (a body the host accepts would trap
the guest) or below a 3x margin, and exits 2 rather than reporting a number
it could not measure.

## Also: `compile --target js` was exiting 70 on main

Not caused by this slice. `cli.clj` called `json/write-str` with
`clojure.data.json`'s variadic kwargs, but the `json.data-json` shim
introduced by "Retire org.clojure/data.json for kotoba-lang/json" takes one
options MAP -- 3 args against arities 1 and 2, so it threw an
ArityException, which is not an ExceptionInfo, so the CLI's `catch
Throwable` printed "internal compiler error" and exited 70 AFTER writing a
good artifact and its .manifest.edn. That also broke the already-landed
`scripts/http-service-e2e.cljs`. Fixed at the two call sites that block js
and evm compiles.

The same mistake is still present at `src/kotoba/compiler/host_profile.clj`
(`:escape-slash`) and three sites in `scripts/perfgate_qualify.clj`. They
are on paths this change does not exercise and are deliberately left alone
rather than fixed untested. The shim's docstring claims "same contract as
clojure.data.json", which is what invited all of them; fixing that at the
root belongs in `kotoba-lang/json`.

---

## Verification (real output, not asserted from reading the code)

**Green:** `approval_queue_test: PASS` — 48/48 assertions, exit 0, against a real `node:http` server over real sockets. State survives across separate requests (`alice` posted in one request is still there in a later one; `alice,bob` meets the minimum). The body is parsed in-guest, including a body whose wanted keys sit behind a nested object containing `{`, `}`, `,` and quotes.

**Deliberate break:** disabling the veto guard (`(and veto ...)` -> `(and false ...)`) produced exactly **one** `NOT OK` — "VETO OUTRANKS THE SATISFIED MINIMUM -> rejected" — and the runner reported `the mutant was CAUGHT (test exited 1)`. The neighbouring "minimum met -> approved" still passed, so the failure came from the veto path that was broken rather than collateral damage.

**Fuel, measured:** worst-case minimum **55,820** units at a 1024-byte body and 1024-byte state; shipped at **262,144** = **4.70x**. The gate discriminates: a copy rewritten to `fuel=20000` reports `FAIL -- the shipped artifact carries 20000 but the worst case this host admits needs 55820`, exit 1. And the consequence is real, not just arithmetic — driving the state to the guest's ceiling returns **500** on the starved artifact where the shipped one returns 200 throughout.

`cloud-itonami-app` was not modified; its files were read only, and its running server on 127.0.0.1:1338 still answers 200.

author: uxdesignlab
body:
## Why

`~/Work/js` was found sitting two commits behind `main` with no clean way to catch it up. The cause was structural, not incidental: both checkouts are **worktrees of one repo**, and git refuses to check out the same branch in two worktrees. `js-dev` holds `main`, so `js` had been left on a **detached HEAD** — a state where `git pull` does not work at all and uncommitted edits are stranded on no branch. It fell behind silently.

## What changed

`js` now runs its own branch, `personal`, tracking `origin/main`. Both agent contracts (`CLAUDE.md` for Claude Code, `AGENTS.md` for Codex) now document:

- **The layout** — which checkout is on which branch, which database, which port, and which one development happens in.
- **The update command for each** — `git pull` in `js-dev`; `git pull --rebase` in `js`, where a local commit puts `personal` ahead of upstream and a plain pull would fail or manufacture merge commits.
- **Why a pull aborts on a dirty `docs/features.md`** — which is most of the time, since this repo requires a docs update in the same change set as every code change. Git aborts safely and never clobbers uncommitted work, but the update silently does not happen, which is the usual reason a checkout is found behind.
- **Not to bare-`git stash` in a worktree** — the stash stack is shared across worktrees and concurrent agent sessions, so `git stash pop` can take someone else's work.
- **That the databases never move** — `data/*` is gitignored, so no git operation can carry real data into the seed-data instance or vice versa. Migrations land on the next app start, not on pull.

Documentation only — no code, no schema, no behavior change.

author: danielguez16
body:
La planche n'a pas pu être lue — le connecteur Design est sans autorisation depuis deux jours. Le brief nommait les corrections assez précisément pour s'en passer ; ce qu'une planche montre et qu'un brief ne dit pas n'a pas été confronté.

## L'ambre revient à la navigation seule

La rangée choisie de la table d'administration était peinte en `brand.50`. Sur une file de quinze lignes, la couleur de marque cesse de dire « ici » pour dire « une ligne parmi d'autres ». Elle passe en matière — `bg.inset` et filet `line.solo` — qui dit la même chose sans dépenser la seule couleur dont la navigation dispose.

Même raison pour trois autres :
- la case cochée de l'arbitrage, qui est de l'ornement répété par rangée ;
- les dix jauges des plans, sur un écran qui se lit et n'offre aucun geste ;
- les onze « Take over » de l'annuaire des salons, qui faisaient de la reprise **la colonne** de l'écran au lieu de son exception — la retenue s'obtient en n'offrant qu'une porte, pas en la peignant.

**Ce qui garde son ambre** : le lien qui ouvre les notes de l'arbitrage. Un lien est un geste, pas de l'ornement, et c'est la seule action du panneau.

## Le texte ne s'entremêle plus

« Ce qui s'ouvre, et rien d'autre » était en capitales espacées de onze points : une étiquette n'a pas de verbe, et une phrase qui en prend le costume se lit deux fois — une fois pour la déchiffrer, une fois pour la comprendre. Elle passait de surcroît sous le seuil de contraste, que onze points en `ink.soft` ne tiennent pas.

Et les poignées quittent le mono : un pseudonyme n'est pas un code lu caractère par caractère. Même défaut que les dates en mono, corrigé la semaine dernière.

## La question ouverte, répondue depuis le code

Design s'inquiétait de « 48 nœuds en mono contre 4 en sans » sur le panneau d'arbitrage. **Le panneau construit en porte un** — le rang d'une tentative. Les quarante-huit sont ceux de la maquette, pas du produit : la densité redoutée n'existe pas ici, et il n'y a donc pas de colonne à retirer.

## Deux mutations, les deux survivantes au premier tour

Rien ne tenait la règle qu'on venait de poser. Une assertion de plus dans l'inventaire de type existant — pas un fichier de garde neuf — portant sur la **table partagée** et non sur les écrans qui l'emploient : c'est là que les quinze occurrences naissent, et un lien d'action doit pouvoir garder son ambre.

118 suites, 1651 tests.

author: onder-akkaya
body:
Follow-up to #1478, which I closed rather than merged.

Dependabot has been rewriting the torch floor to `torch>=2.13.0+cpu,<3.0`. That isn't a valid PEP 440 requirement — a local version label (`+cpu`) is only permitted on `==` or `!=` — so `backend/requirements.txt` stops parsing entirely and import-guard fails the PR:

```
packaging.requirements.InvalidRequirement: Local version label can only be used with `==` or `!=` operators
    torch>=2.13.0+cpu,<3.0
         ~~~~~~~~^
```

Reproduces identically in CI (run `32684118943`) and locally against the repo's own `packaging`.

## Why it happens

Two lines above the torch pin:

```
--extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
torch>=2.13.0,<3.0  # CPU-only wheel via pytorch whl index ...; no +cpu here, pip rejects a local version label on a >= specifier
```

That index resolves torch to the CPU-variant wheel, so the *installed* version reports as `2.13.0+cpu`. Dependabot reads the installed version and copies it into the floor. The line's own trailing comment already warned about this — dependabot just doesn't read comments.

Left alone, it regenerates on every torch release. #1478 was at least the second occurrence.

## What changed

One `ignore` entry on the `pip` / `/backend` block, listing all three `version-update:semver-*` types. That suppresses version bumps for torch and nothing else — **security advisories still open PRs**, which is the property that made me comfortable adding an ignore at all rather than closing the PR by hand each month.

The comment in the config explains the mechanism so the next person doesn't remove it as unexplained cruft.

## Verification

- `yaml.safe_load` on the edited file parses, and the `ignore` block lands on the `/backend` pip entry (not one of the other four ecosystems).
- No change to `backend/requirements.txt`; the torch floor stays bare, which is the correct form. Picking the CPU wheel is the index's job, not the specifier's.

Narrow scope on purpose — this is CI wiring, so it's a PR rather than a direct push, and it's split from #1493 (the `environment.yml` alignment) because they're separate changes that happen to share an afternoon.

author: ajit-zer07
body:
## What

Bumps the `conformance` CI job's pinned spec ref from `bff3cf3afbdcea619834916e8f0bcac7e82ba658` to `31cf8743b62debe2c7c8572ce3a3a0b7ca5ad099` in `.github/workflows/ci.yml:146`, and retargets two doc-comments in `crates/acdp-registry-server/tests/conformance.rs` (`:538`, `:1171`) that name the old SHA. `CONTRIBUTING.md` needs no edit — it only points at the pin's location, not its value.

This is **Phase 1 of a 5-PR wave** (REG-2 · REG-5 · REG-6 · REG-8 · REG-9, `plans/reg2-reg5-reg6-reg8-reg9-wave4.md`), landed alone per `plans/00-overview.md` §6 hazard **H6**: never bump a pinned spec SHA in the same PR as a fixture/behavior change. A reviewer sees "we adopted a newer spec" independently of "and here is what we found once we did" — and a green conformance run on *this* PR is unambiguous evidence the pin itself is inert, not that compensating code is masking a break.

## Why this pin

`31cf874` is the spec repo's current `main` HEAD, which includes the promotion of **RFC-ACDP-0015 to Final (0.4.0)**:
- `invalid_witness_cosignature` error code: Proposed → **Stable** (502, distinct from `invalid_log_proof`, fixture `wit-004`)
- `acdp-log-witness` profile: Draft → **Final**
- `retracted`/`republished` lifecycle codes and the `key-revocation` context type also move Proposed → Stable at this pin

This unblocks REG-2/REG-5 (the rest of this wave, PR B) and REG-1's original acceptance criteria, which pinned pre-promotion.

## The diff at this pin is annotation-only — verified, not assumed

`bff3cf3a → 31cf874` touches 11 files under `schemas/`+`registries/`, all `M`, **zero added/removed/renamed** (14 insertions, 14 deletions). Six fixture files changed only a generator path inside a `description` string (`temp/gen-*.py` → `scripts/gen-*.py`). `registries/profiles.json` changed exactly one value: `acdp-log-witness.spec_reference` `"(0.4.0, Draft)"` → `"(0.4.0, Final)"`. No `fixture_families` key, `id`, `request`, `expected`, or `applies_to_profiles` changed anywhere. The rest is status-annotation prose in `error-codes.md`/`profiles.md`/`lifecycle-event-types.md`/`context-types.md`.

## Local evidence (pinned worktree — never the live spec tree)

```
$ git -C /Users/ajitkoti/code/agentcontextdistributionprotocol/agentcontextdistributionprotocol worktree add /tmp/acdp-spec-pin 31cf874
$ ACDP_REQUIRE_CONFORMANCE=1 ACDP_SPEC_DIR=/tmp/acdp-spec-pin \
    cargo test -p acdp-registry-server --features storage-sqlite,playground \
    --test conformance --test conformance_gate -- --nocapture
...
conformance: replayed 4 exchange(s); failures=0
conformance: ran by family:
  - pub: 3
  - ret: 1
```

author: pandermatt
body:
Walky has no backend and fetches nothing from a third party, so every byte
the page can ask for is already in the build output. A service worker
precaches all of it on install and serves cache-first, which makes offline
a guarantee rather than a degraded mode.

The precache list is generated by a small Vite plugin instead of being kept
by hand: Rollup's filenames carry a content hash, so a hand-written list is
stale after the first edit, and a list one file short is a missing toolbar
icon on the plane. The plugin takes the emitted bundle plus everything
copied from public/, drops the worker itself, and substitutes both the list
and a hash of its contents into src/sw.ts. That hash names the cache, so a
new build lands in a new cache and the old one is dropped on activation.

An update is offered, never applied on its own -- the map you drew lives in
memory and nowhere else, so a self-reloading worker would throw away the
crowd you were watching. The page shows a chip with a Reload button; a first
install says it is ready to run offline and dismisses itself.

Also here:

- A web app manifest and the icons it needs, derived from images/icon.png:
  the original pedestrian glyph painted white on #1E1E1E, since a black
  glyph on transparency vanishes against a dark home screen. The maskable
  one keeps the figure inside the inner 80% of the square.
- iOS reads almost none of the manifest, so the home-screen icon, app name
  and standalone mode each get their own tag in index.html.
- Installed, the page runs edge to edge, so the toolbar and the panels are
  offset by env(safe-area-inset-*) rather than sitting under a notch.
- _headers keeps sw.js revalidated, which is how a new build reaches anyone
  still holding the old one.

Verified in Chromium against a server that mimics the production headers:
a browser launched with no network at all loads the app from cache with
zero failed requests, draws walls, paints a crowd and runs the simulation;
reloads offline keep working; and a second build produces the update chip
and retires the previous cache.

author: mutkuoz
body:
The README described the project as a checklist of what did and did not exist. Everything in that "Not yet" table is now built, so the table is gone and the document explains the thing instead: what it is, why the two-repo shape follows from putting notes in a git repo, the five setup steps with the Pages caveat that trips everyone, and how to use what is there. Screenshots of the real app, light and dark, are in docs/media/.

Writing "images over 1600px or 1MB are downscaled" turned out to be half false. prepareImage consulted the downscaler only above a megabyte, so a 4000px screenshot that compressed to 300KB was uploaded at full size -- the pixel half of the rule never ran. Only the downscaler can measure pixels, since it is the thing that decodes, so it is now always called and returns the original when there is nothing to do.

That makes the decode reachable for any pasted file, including bytes that claim to be a PNG and are not, so canvasDownscaler no longer lets a decode failure escape: shrinking is an optimisation, and losing the paste is a worse outcome than uploading the original.
